reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Many drugs prolong the QT interval and predispose to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation
Common culprits include certain antiarrhythmics, macrolide and fluoroquinolone antibiotics, antipsychotics, methadone and some antiemetics
Risk is compounded by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia, female sex and underlying cardiac disease
Concomitant use of multiple QT-prolonging drugs or agents that inhibit their metabolism greatly increases risk
The mechanism is blockade of the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr) carried by the hERG channel, delaying repolarisation
Torsades often follows a short-long-short RR sequence and may present with palpitations, syncope or cardiac arrest
Management includes stopping offending drugs, correcting electrolytes, intravenous magnesium and increasing heart rate (pacing or isoprenaline) to shorten the QT
Always calculate a rate-corrected QT (QTc) and reassess after starting or changing high-risk drugs
reference.pathophysiology: Ventricular repolarisation depends heavily on the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr) conducted by the hERG channel. Many structurally diverse drugs block this channel, prolonging the action potential duration and the QT interval on the surface electrocardiogram. Delayed repolarisation predisposes to early afterdepolarisations, which can trigger torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis. Susceptibility is increased when repolarisation reserve is already reduced by electrolyte disturbance (particularly low potassium, magnesium or calcium), bradycardia, structural heart disease, or subclinical congenital long QT mutations. Drug interactions that raise plasma levels of a QT-prolonging agent, or combine several such agents, further impair repolarisation and heighten arrhythmic risk.
additionalDifferentials: Electrolyte disturbance causing QT prolongation independent of drugs
Other causes of syncope (vasovagal, structural heart disease, heart block)
Hypothermia or raised intracranial pressure affecting the QT
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with QTc calculation and serial monitoring
Review of all medications for QT-prolonging agents and interactions
Continuous cardiac (telemetry) monitoring in high-risk patients
Renal and hepatic function affecting drug clearance
Consideration of genetic testing where congenital long QT is suspected
redFlags: Documented torsades de pointes or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Syncope or presyncope in a patient with a markedly prolonged QTc
Progressive QTc prolongation after starting a culprit drug
Severe electrolyte disturbance compounding QT prolongation
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition, drug withdrawal and correction of precipitants, the QT usually normalises and the arrhythmic risk resolves. Untreated torsades can be rapidly fatal, but appropriately managed episodes generally have a good outcome.
pitfalls: Prescribing additional QT-prolonging drugs without reviewing existing therapy
Overlooking hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia that markedly amplifies risk
Relying on the uncorrected QT rather than a rate-corrected QTc
Missing drug interactions that raise plasma concentrations of a QT-prolonging agent
Failing to monitor the electrocardiogram after initiating a high-risk medication
management: Immediately stop the offending QT-prolonging drug and avoid concomitant QT-prolonging agents and interacting drugs that raise its plasma levels
Correct and replete electrolytes, particularly potassium, magnesium and calcium, to restore repolarisation reserve
Treat torsades de pointes with intravenous magnesium sulphate and correction of precipitants, and defibrillate sustained or haemodynamically unstable episodes
For recurrent or bradycardia- and pause-dependent torsades, raise the heart rate with overdrive pacing or an isoprenaline infusion
Monitor with serial twelve-lead ECG QTc measurement and continuous telemetry in high-risk patients
Review renal and hepatic function affecting drug clearance and refer to cardiology, considering congenital long-QT testing where suspected
